content: Adrenaline and vasopressin are commonly used in the management of cardiac arrest, but there is ongoing uncertainty regarding their safety, efficacy, and optimal dosing. The objective of this review was to evaluate whether the administration of adrenaline, vasopressin, or a combination of both during cardiac arrest provides any survival benefit. The review included randomized controlled trials comparing standard-dose adrenaline with placebo, standard-dose adrenaline with high-dose adrenaline, and adrenaline with vasopressin in both adult and pediatric populations experiencing cardiac arrest. A total of 26 studies involving 21,704 participants were analyzed. The quality of evidence for each outcome was assessed using the GRADE approach. Moderate-quality evidence demonstrated that standard-dose adrenaline increased survival to hospital discharge compared to placebo. Specifically, the survival rate increased from 23 per 1000 to 32 per 1000 (risk ratio [RR] 1.44, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.11 to 1.86). However, the evidence was of very low quality regarding survival to hospital discharge when comparing high-dose adrenaline to standard-dose adrenaline, as well as when comparing standard-dose adrenaline to vasopressin or to a combination of adrenaline and vasopressin. Moderate-quality evidence also showed that standard-dose adrenaline improved survival to hospital admission compared to placebo, with survival increasing from 83 per 1000 to 209 per 1000 (RR 2.51, 95% CI 1.67 to 3.76). However, the evidence was very low quality for comparisons between standard-dose and high-dose adrenaline. Vasopressin, when compared to standard-dose adrenaline, may improve survival to hospital admission (RR 1.27, 95% CI 1.04 to 1.54; low-quality evidence), with survival increasing from 260 per 1000 to 330 per 1000. However, vasopressin appeared to make little or no difference when compared to a combination of standard-dose adrenaline and vasopressin (RR 0.95, 95% CI 0.83 to 1.08; low-quality evidence). There was no evidence to suggest that adrenaline (at any dose) or vasopressin improved neurological outcomes. Moderate-quality evidence indicated that standard-dose adrenaline increased the rate of return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC) compared to placebo, with ROSC rates increasing from 115 per 1000 to 329 per 1000 (RR 2.86, 95% CI 2.21 to 3.71). However, the evidence was very low quality for comparisons of ROSC between standard-dose and high-dose adrenaline, as well as between standard-dose adrenaline and vasopressin. Standard-dose adrenaline may make little or no difference to ROSC when compared to a combination of standard-dose adrenaline and vasopressin (RR 0.97, 95% CI 0.87 to 1.08; low-quality evidence). The source of funding was not disclosed in 11 of the 26 studies. In four studies, the study drugs were provided by the manufacturer, although neither adrenaline nor vasopressin represents a commercially profitable option. The remaining 11 studies were funded by research foundations or government organizations. In conclusion, this review provides moderate-quality evidence that standard-dose adrenaline improves ROSC, survival to hospital admission, and survival to hospital discharge when compared to placebo. However, there is low-quality evidence suggesting that it does not improve survival with favorable neurological outcomes. Very low-quality evidence suggests that high-dose adrenaline compared to standard-dose adrenaline may improve ROSC and survival to admission. Vasopressin, when compared to standard-dose adrenaline, may improve survival to admission but does not appear to improve ROSC. The combination of adrenaline and vasopressin does not seem to provide additional benefits over adrenaline alone. Importantly, many of the included studies were conducted over 20 years ago, and changes in treatment practices since then may limit the applicability of these findings to current clinical practice.
